goldens.comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.

The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.

parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.

When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.

The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

When credential sharing is enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response object, but the code accesses res?.data which doesn't exist on Response, causing token to be undefined and throwing a TypeError on the next line

parseRefreshTokenResponse uses z.string().toString() and z.string().optional().toString() as computed object keys, which both evaluate to the same string '[object Object]', causing the second to override the first and the schema to only validate access_token instead of the intended any-number-valued-property semantics

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`, `minimumTokenResponseSchema` is defined with computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]`. Those expressions are evaluated immediately when building the object literal, producing a single string key (very likely the same string for both), so the latter entry overwrites the former. As a result, the schema does not implement an index-signature-like “any number-valued property” check; it effectively only requires `access_token` (and at most one oddly named property), and other response fields are not validated as intended. This is a concrete correctness bug in the diff.

app-credential webhook handler has no try/catch, so ZodError from schema parse, symmetricDecrypt errors, and JSON.parse errors bypass the API error contract and surface as 500s leaking internals to the caller
FindFirst-then-update-or-create flow in app-credential webhook is not atomic, allowing concurrent webhook deliveries to create duplicate credentials for the same user/app pair

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the handler does `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` and then either `update` (by `id`) or `create`. This check-then-act sequence is not wrapped in a transaction and does not use an `upsert` on a unique constraint, so two concurrent webhook requests for the same `(userId, appId)` can both observe “no credential” and both execute `create`, resulting in duplicate credentials. The inline comment (“Can't use prisma upsert...”) further indicates there may not be a usable unique constraint to prevent this.

adjudication_records.issue_text: parseRefreshTokenResponse throws a generic Error discarding both the Zod error and the upstream response, making malformed token responses undiagnosable in production

adjudication.rationale: In the new `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`, the function does `schema.safeParse(response)` (or `minimumTokenResponseSchema.safeParse(response)`) and if it fails it throws `new Error("Invalid refreshed tokens were returned")` without including `refreshTokenResponse.error` (the Zod error) or the offending `response`. This is a verifiable loss of diagnostic information introduced in the diff, unlike the previous Office365 code path which logged Zod/MS response details.

adjudication_records.issue_text: APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED evaluates to the value of the encryption key string instead of a boolean, so operators setting CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET='false' will silently enable the feature instead of disabling it

adjudication.rationale: The diff only shows `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` being imported from `@calcom/lib/constants` and used in boolean contexts (e.g., `if (!APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED)`). The diff does not define how `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` is computed, nor does it show it being derived from the encryption key or any env var. Also, the claim about `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET='false'` enabling the feature is not supported by the shown logic: the webhook secret is only used for header comparison after the feature-gate check, and whether `'false'` is truthy/falsey is irrelevant because it’s compared for equality, not coerced to boolean. Therefore the proposed finding is not verifiable from, and is inconsistent with, the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Office365 CalendarService lost the diagnostic logging of tokenResponse.error and responseJson that existed in the previous implementation, making O365 token refresh failures opaque in production

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts`, the previous implementation did `refreshTokenResponseSchema.safeParse(responseJson)` and, on failure, executed a `console.error(...)` that included both `tokenResponse.error` and the raw `responseJson`. In the new code, this is replaced with `parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseJson, refreshTokenResponseSchema)`, and the explicit `if (!tokenResponse.success) { console.error(...) }` block is removed. `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws a generic `Error("Invalid refreshed tokens were returned")` on parse failure, so the detailed diagnostic logging present before is lost, making failures less observable from this code path.

adjudication_records.issue_text: CalendarService.ts:91 stores Zod SafeParseReturnType wrapper as the credential key instead of the parsed credentials, causing subsequent reads of credential.key.access_token to return undefined

adjudication.rationale: Real issue. In `packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts`, the refreshed credentials are now saved as `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema);` and written to Prisma (`data: { key }`). But `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the Zod `safeParse` result object (`{ success, data, error }`), not the parsed credential object (`.data`). This means `credential.key` in the DB will become the wrapper, so later code expecting `credential.key.access_token` would see `undefined` (it would be under `credential.key.data.access_token`).

This matches the golden concern about inconsistent return shape and resulting crash.

adjudication_records.issue_text: refreshOAuthTokens.ts:8-17: Inconsistent return type (fetch Response when sync enabled vs axios/parsed object when disabled) breaks Hubspot, Zoho Bigin, Zoho CRM, and Google adapters on the sync path

adjudication.rationale:
Yes. `refreshOAuthTokens` returns different shapes depending on the sync path: when `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT && userId` it returns a `fetch(...)` `Response`, otherwise it returns whatever `refreshFunction()` returns. Call sites assume specific non-Response types:
- GoogleCalendarService now does `const res = await refreshOAuthTokens(...); const token = res?.data;` but a `fetch` `Response` has no `.data`, so on the sync path `token` becomes `undefined` and `token.access_token`/`token.expiry_date` will throw.
- HubspotCalendarService types the result as `HubspotToken` and immediately uses it as such; on the sync path it would instead receive a `Response` object, breaking downstream logic.
The mention of Zoho adapters isn’t verifiable from this diff, but the underlying inconsistent return type problem is real and demonstrably breaks at least Google + Hubspot on the sync path.

adjudication_records.issue_text: parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:5-13: The minimum token schema uses bogus computed keys where z.string().toString() yields '[object Object]', causing the second key to overwrite the first and skipping numeric expiry validation
matched_golden_ids: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both comments flag the same underlying bug: the Zod schema is built with computed property keys derived from `z.string().toString()`/`z.string().optional().toString()`, producing invalid/meaningless keys (e.g., "[object Object]") and breaking the schema definition. The candidate adds the overwrite/validation-skipping effect, which is a consequence of the same incorrect computed-key usage highlighted in the golden comment.

adjudication_records.issue_text: parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:24-26: Injects a literal string 'refresh_token' as the refresh_token value when the sync endpoint omits it, causing downstream code to use a bogus token
app-credential.ts:15-20: Webhook secret compared with !== which is timing-unsafe; should use crypto.timingSafeEqual to avoid leaking prefix information

adjudication.rationale:
In apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts the webhook authentication is implemented as a direct string inequality check:

```ts
if (req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME || "calcom-webhook-secret"] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET)
```

Using `!==` on attacker-controlled input vs a secret can result in non-constant-time comparisons (typical string equality checks may short-circuit on first differing character), which is the class of issue the finding describes. A constant-time compare (e.g., `crypto.timingSafeEqual` over Buffers of equal length) is the standard mitigation for this pattern.

While practical exploitation over the network may be difficult/noisy, the diff does introduce the timing-unsafe secret comparison as stated.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app-credential.ts:29,55-57: Webhook trusts arbitrary userId from request body, allowing any holder of the shared secret to create or overwrite credentials for any user (IDOR)

adjudication.rationale: The new API route `/api/webhook/app-credential.ts` authenticates requests only by comparing a single shared secret in a header against `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` (lines around the header check). After that, it accepts `userId` from the request body (`reqBody.userId`) and directly performs `prisma.credential.findFirst` / `update` or `create` for that `userId` without any additional authorization tying the caller to that specific user. As a result, anyone who knows the shared webhook secret can create or overwrite credentials for any Cal.com user ID (IDOR-style impact), because `userId` is fully caller-controlled.

adjudication_records.issue_text: zoho-bigin/lib/CalendarService.ts:88: Passes credentialId instead of credential.userId to refreshOAuthTokens, causing the sync endpoint to operate against the wrong principal

salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts:75-97: Token refresh is performed in constructor on every instantiation but the refreshed token is not used to build jsforce.Connection, doubling refresh traffic and using stale token
matched_golden_ids: The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both describe the same core bug: after performing a token refresh, the code still constructs `jsforce.Connection` using the pre-refresh `credentialKey.access_token`/`instance_url`, resulting in use of stale credentials (and potential auth/data issues). The candidate additionally notes unnecessary refresh traffic, but the main issue matches the golden comment.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app-credential.ts:11: No HTTP method restriction; handler processes any method including GET which will throw on z.parse(undefined) when body is absent

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the handler never checks `req.method` (e.g., only allowing POST). After the header secret check passes, it unconditionally runs `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)`. For methods like GET (or POST without a body / wrong content-type), `req.body` can be `undefined`/empty, causing Zod `.parse` to throw and the route to return a 500 instead of a controlled 405/400. This is a verifiable correctness/robustness issue introduced by the new endpoint.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app-credential.ts:29,55: Unhandled throws from ZodError and JSON.parse leak as 500s; should use safeParse and guard decrypt/parse operations

adjudication.rationale: In apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts the handler calls appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body) without a try/catch. zod `parse` throws on invalid input, which will bubble up and cause a 500 response. Later it does `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` with no guarding; both `symmetricDecrypt` (e.g., missing/invalid key or bad ciphertext) and `JSON.parse` can throw, likewise resulting in an unhandled exception and 500. There is no error handling middleware shown in this diff for this route, so the finding is a concrete, verifiable defect introduced by the new file.

adjudication_records.issue_text: salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts:91: if (response.statusText !== 'OK') is fragile since statusText varies by server/locale; should use response.ok or response.status

adjudication.rationale: The proposed finding points to `salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts:91` and claims there is an `if (response.statusText !== 'OK')` check. In the provided diff, the Salesforce CalendarService changes shown only add `zod` import, `parseRefreshTokenResponse` import, and a `salesforceTokenSchema` definition, then the file is truncated before any `fetch`/`response` handling code is visible. adjudication_records.issue_text: app-credential.ts:56: Decryption key falls back to empty string when env var is unset; a future refactor could silently decrypt with empty string, should validate key length explicitly

adjudication.rationale:
In the newly added `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the decryption call explicitly falls back to an empty string when `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` is unset:

```ts
symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY || "")
```

There is no validation that the env var is present or that it matches the documented required length (comment in `.env.example` says 32 bytes for AES256). This means the handler can proceed into decryption with `""` as the key, which is a concrete correctness/security risk in the current diff (not merely a future refactor concern).

adjudication_records.issue_text: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the full safeParse wrapper object { success, data, error } instead of .data, corrupting stored credentials so that subsequent token fields (access_token, refresh_token, expiry_date) are all undefined on next load
matched_golden_ids: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate flags that parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the Zod safeParse wrapper ({success, data, error}) and that storing it (instead of the parsed payload in .data or using parse) corrupts persisted credentials, matching the golden issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses invalid computed keys (z.string().toString() evaluates to '[object Object]'), causing the two computed keys to collide and the schema to only validate access_token while stripping all other fields (refresh_token, expiry_date, expires_in, etc.)

adjudication.rationale: Yes. In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`, `minimumTokenResponseSchema` is declared as `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), [z.string().toString()]: z.number(), [z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional() })`. Those computed property names are evaluated to strings at runtime (very likely `"[object Object]"` or similarly non-meaningful strings), not to an index signature. This does not create “any key with a number” behavior; instead it creates one (or two) literal property names, and the required `[z.string().toString()]` number field will almost certainly be missing from real OAuth responses, causing `safeParse` to fail and the function to throw `Invalid refreshed tokens were returned` in the credential-sharing path. The finding’s core claim (computed keys are invalid / collide and don’t validate intended fields) reflects a real defect introduced by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: parseRefreshTokenResponse replaces a missing refresh_token with the literal string 'refresh_token' instead of preserving the existing refresh token, destroying valid refresh tokens for OAuth providers that don't return a new refresh_token on every refresh
matched_golden_ids: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both describe the same bug: parseRefreshTokenResponse assigns the literal string 'refresh_token' when the field is missing in the refresh response, instead of keeping the existing refresh token. This corrupts/invalidates the refresh token and leads to authentication/refresh failures.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Outbound fetch to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT has no timeout/AbortController, no retry/backoff, no response-status check, and no body parsing, causing indefinite blocking on the hot path of calendar operations when the endpoint is slow or hangs

adjudication.rationale: The new helper `refreshOAuthTokens` (packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts) performs `await fetch(process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, ...)` without any timeout/AbortController. If that endpoint is slow or never responds, the awaited promise can hang and block token refresh paths that are called during calendar operations. In the same function, the response is returned as a raw `Response` with no `response.ok` check and no body parsing; callers must handle it but at least one caller does not: GoogleCalendarService uses `const token = res?.data;` which will be `undefined` for a Fetch `Response`, demonstrating the lack of parsing/shape checking is a real defect introduced in this diff. Retry/backoff is not implemented either (more of a robustness gap than a strict bug).

adjudication_records.issue_text: refreshOAuthTokens return-type contract mismatch: returns a fetch Response when credential sync is on but the wrapped library result when off, breaking multiple callers (Google, Hubspot, Zoho Bigin, Zoho CRM) that expect non-Response shapes with .data property

adjudication.rationale: `refreshOAuthTokens` has an inconsistent return contract: when sync is enabled it returns a native `fetch` `Response`, but when disabled it returns whatever `refreshFunction()` returns (often a parsed object or a library-specific response). This is verifiably breaking in the diff: (1) `GoogleCalendarService` calls `refreshOAuthTokens(...)` and then does `const token = res?.data;`—a `fetch` `Response` has no `.data`, so token extraction will fail under sync mode. (2) `HubspotCalendarService` types the result as `HubspotToken` and uses it as token data, but under sync mode it will receive a `Response` object (not JSON-parsed), so the type/shape is wrong and subsequent field access will break unless additional parsing is done. The finding’s mention of Zoho is not evidenced in this diff, but the core mismatch issue is real based on Google + Hubspot changes shown here.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does not show any Salesforce token refresh logic using `response.statusText !== 'OK'` (or any `statusText` checks at all). adjudication_records.issue_text: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the full SafeParseResult ({success, data}) instead of just the parsed data, so the DB stores {"success": true, "data": {...}} instead of {...}, breaking credential.key.access_token access on next read

adjudication.rationale:
In packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts the function builds `refreshTokenResponse` via `schema.safeParse(...)` / `minimumTokenResponseSchema.safeParse(...)` and then returns `refreshTokenResponse` directly. That return value is a Zod SafeParseResult shaped like `{ success: boolean, data?: ... , error?: ... }`, not the parsed data object.

In the diff, GoogleCalendarService uses it as if it returns the credential key object: `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema); await prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`. That will store the SafeParseResult wrapper in `credential.key` (e.g. `{ success: true, data: {...} }`) instead of the actual keys object, which would break subsequent code expecting `credential.key.access_token` etc.

(Office365CalendarService, by contrast, treats the return as a SafeParseResult: it checks `.success` and uses `.data`, so it would not be affected.)

adjudication_records.issue_text: refresh_token is defaulted to the literal string "refresh_token" when the response omits it, corrupting stored credentials by overwriting real refresh tokens with garbage

adjudication.rationale: Yes. In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`, if the parsed token response lacks `refresh_token`, the code forcibly sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. When credential sharing + `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` are enabled, the function uses `minimumTokenResponseSchema` (which does not require `refresh_token`), so this branch can trigger for normal refresh responses that omit refresh_token. This value then flows into persisted credentials in at least `Office365CalendarService`: it calls `parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseJson, refreshTokenResponseSchema)` and then merges `tokenResponse.data` into `o365AuthCredentials`, which would overwrite a previously valid `refresh_token` with the literal string, and then writes the updated credentials back to Prisma. That is a concrete credential-corruption defect introduced by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses z.string().toString() as computed keys which both evaluate to "[object Object]", causing the second to override the first and losing all expiry field validation

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`, `minimumTokenResponseSchema` is declared as `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), [z.string().toString()]: z.number(), [z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional() })`. In a JS object literal, computed keys are evaluated immediately to strings; `z.string()` / `z.string().optional()` are objects, and calling `.toString()` on them yields the same string (typically `"[object Object]"`). That means both computed properties target the same literal key and the latter overrides the former, so the intended “any numeric expiry field” validation is not achieved (it instead defines a single `"[object Object]"` property, likely optional/unknown after override). This is a concrete correctness bug introduced by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: refreshOAuthTokens returns a raw fetch() Response in sync mode instead of the type callers expect (HubspotToken, axios response, google-auth response), breaking every caller when sync is enabled
matched_golden_ids: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate flags the same core bug: in sync-enabled mode the refresh helper returns the raw fetch Response rather than the integration-specific token/response object that callers (e.g., Hubspot/Google refreshAccessToken) expect, leading to runtime breakage unless return type/call sites are adjusted.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app-credential webhook handler has no HTTP method restriction, allowing GET/DELETE/PUT to trigger credential creation/update, exposing it to CSRF-style attacks

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the `handler` never checks `req.method` (e.g., only allowing POST). As written, any HTTP method (GET/PUT/DELETE/etc.) will execute the same credential update/create logic as long as the caller supplies the expected secret header and a body that passes the zod schema. So the endpoint is not method-restricted and can be triggered via non-POST methods. The "CSRF-style" framing is less direct because a secret header is required, but the lack of method restriction itself is a verifiable issue in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body) throws unhandled ZodError on malformed input, producing a 500 with potential schema detail leakage instead of a clean 400

adjudication.rationale: In the new API route `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the handler calls `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` without a surrounding try/catch or error handling middleware. `zod.parse(...)` throws a `ZodError` on malformed input, which in a Next.js API route will typically bubble up and produce a 500 response (and in non-production may include error details). There is no explicit logic to return a clean 400 for validation failures, so the finding is verifiably present in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: CalendarService.ts stores SafeParseResult object as credential key instead of parsed credentials, breaking Google Calendar on every token refresh

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts`, the refreshed credentials are now persisted as `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema);` and then `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`. However, `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the *safeParse result object* (`{ success, data/error }`), not the parsed credentials (`.data`). So the DB `credential.key` will be a SafeParseResult wrapper rather than the expected credential payload, which will break subsequent reads/uses of the credential key (and thus token refresh/usage).

adjudication_records.issue_text: refreshOAuthTokens.ts returns raw fetch Response in sync mode, but callers expect typed token objects/Axios responses, breaking OAuth refresh across all adapters

adjudication.rationale:
Yes. In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts`, the sync-mode branch (`APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT && userId`) returns the raw `fetch(...)` `Response` object. But at least some callers treat the return value as a parsed/typed token response:
- `packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` assigns `const res = await refreshOAuthTokens(...)` and then does `const token = res?.data;` (gaxios-style). A `fetch` `Response` has no `.data`, so `token` becomes `undefined`, breaking refresh.
- `packages/app-store/hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts` types the result as `HubspotToken` and will receive a `Response` in sync-mode, also breaking downstream usage.
Other adapters that already expect a `fetch` `Response` (e.g., Office365) may still work, but the mismatch is a real, verifiable defect introduced by the diff for those expecting non-Response token objects.

adjudication_records.issue_text: refreshOAuthTokens.ts fetch to sync endpoint has no timeout, no response.ok check, no retry, and no error logging

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts`, the branch that calls the credential sync endpoint does a plain `fetch(process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, { method: "POST", body: new URLSearchParams(...) })` and immediately returns the `Response` without checking `response.ok`/status, without any try/catch or logging on failure, and without any timeout/abort mechanism or retry logic. These omissions are directly verifiable in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Zoho-Bigin CalendarService.ts passes credentialId instead of credential.userId to refreshOAuthTokens, causing sync endpoint to receive wrong user identifier

adjudication_records.issue_text: app-credential.ts uses schema.parse(req.body) without safeParse/try-catch, causing unhandled 500 with stack trace on malformed input

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the handler does `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` with no surrounding try/catch and without using `safeParse`. Zod’s `parse` throws on malformed input, and the function does not handle that exception, so a bad request body will result in an unhandled error and Next.js will respond with a 500 rather than a controlled 4xx. (Whether a stack trace is returned to the client depends on Next.js dev vs production mode, but the unhandled 500 behavior is directly verifiable from the diff.)

adjudication_records.issue_text: app-credential.ts JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...)) is unguarded, throwing unhandled 500 on malformed ciphertext, wrong/empty key, or invalid JSON

adjudication.rationale: In the new `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the handler does `const keys = JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY || ""));` without any try/catch or validation. If `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` is missing/empty (it explicitly falls back to `""`), if `reqBody.keys` is not valid ciphertext for that key, if `symmetricDecrypt` throws, or if it returns a non-JSON string, `JSON.parse` will throw. There is no error handling around this, so the route will error out and return an unhandled 500 instead of a controlled 4xx/meaningful response.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app-credential.ts findFirst + create has a race condition with no unique constraint, transaction, or upsert, allowing duplicate credentials for same (userId, appId)

adjudication.rationale: In apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts the logic is "findFirst" by (userId, appId) and then either update or create. This is a classic non-atomic read-then-write sequence with no transaction/locking, so two concurrent requests for the same userId/appSlug can both see no existing credential and both execute create. Whether this results in duplicate rows or a unique-constraint error depends on schema (not shown in the diff), but the race condition itself is clearly present in the added code.

Salesforce CalendarService.ts uses response.statusText !== 'OK' as success check, which fails on HTTP/2 (empty statusText) and non-'OK' reason phrases on valid 200 responses

adjudication_records.issue_text: parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts swallows Zod error and original response into generic error message, removing diagnostic logging that previously existed in the Office365 path

adjudication.rationale: In `Office365CalendarService.ts`, the previous code did `refreshTokenResponseSchema.safeParse(responseJson)` and, on failure, logged `tokenResponse.error` and the raw `responseJson` via `console.error(...)`. adjudication_records.issue_text: parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts: Zod schema uses computed keys [z.string().toString()] which produce '[object Object]' for both keys, causing the second to silently overwrite the first, resulting in a schema that only validates access_token

adjudication.rationale: In packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts, the schema defines computed keys as `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]`. `z.string()` returns a Zod type object, so `.toString()` evaluates to the same string (typically "[object Object]") for both computed properties. That means the second property definition overwrites the first at object-literal construction time, so the intended "any numeric expiry field" constraint is lost (and you effectively end up with only one "[object Object]" key plus `access_token`). This is a concrete correctness bug in the diff; it will not validate arbitrary expiry-number fields as intended.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Webhook secret check uses non-constant-time !== comparison, leaking secret length/prefix via timing, and has auth-bypass risk when CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET is unset
symmetricDecrypt falls back to empty string when CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY is missing, which will either throw or produce garbage data stored as credentials

adjudication_records.issue_text: Webhook handler has no req.method === 'POST' guard, allowing any HTTP verb to create or overwrite user credentials

adjudication.rationale: In the new API route `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the handler processes requests (parses `req.body`, decrypts keys, and performs `prisma.credential.update/create`) without any `req.method` check (e.g., `if (req.method !== "POST") ...`). Next.js API routes can be invoked with any HTTP verb unless explicitly guarded, so a request using GET/PUT/PATCH/DELETE with the correct secret header could still reach the credential write logic. This matches the finding that any verb is allowed to create/overwrite credentials.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Webhook handler's .parse(req.body) is uncaught, producing a 500 with raw ZodError instead of a 400 for malformed bodies
matched_golden_ids: The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both describe the same issue: using Zod's schema.parse on the webhook request body without catching validation errors causes exceptions that surface as 500 Internal Server Errors instead of returning a 400 Bad Request for malformed payloads.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Salesforce refresh logic runs in the service constructor instead of refreshAccessToken, causing a network round-trip and DB write on every calendar operation

adjudication.rationale: The diff excerpt for `packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts` only shows new imports (`z`, `parseRefreshTokenResponse`) and the addition of `salesforceTokenSchema`, but it does not include the constructor implementation, any `refreshAccessToken` function, or any logic that performs a refresh/network call/DB write. Without seeing code that moved refresh logic into the constructor (or evidence of a DB write in the constructor), the claim is not verifiable from this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Salesforce doesn't use the new refreshOAuthTokens helper, silently excluding it from the credential-sync feature

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, SalesforceCalendarService only shows a new `zod` import, an added `salesforceTokenSchema`, and an added import of `parseRefreshTokenResponse`; there is no visible token-refresh logic in the provided hunk to verify whether Salesforce does or does not refresh tokens, nor any place where `refreshOAuthTokens` should clearly be used. While it’s true that the shown Salesforce file does not import/use `refreshOAuthTokens` (unlike other integrations), the claim that this “silently excludes it from the credential-sync feature” is not a verifiable defect from the diff alone because the relevant refresh flow isn’t shown and it may be intentional or handled elsewhere (e.g., via jsforce internals).

adjudication_records.issue_text: parseRefreshTokenResponse mutates the parsed result and injects the literal string 'refresh_token' as a placeholder, which could be persisted to DB and break subsequent refresh attempts

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`, the function explicitly mutates the parsed data: if `refresh_token` is missing it sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. In `packages/app-store/office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts`, the parsed token response is merged into persisted credentials via `o365AuthCredentials = { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...(tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data) }` and then saved with `prisma.credential.update(...)`. If the refresh response omits `refresh_token` (common in OAuth refresh flows), this placeholder string will override the real stored refresh token and get persisted, breaking future refresh attempts. This risk is directly introduced by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Office365 and Zoom callers still check .success on parseRefreshTokenResponse return value even though it always throws on failure, creating dead code that misleads maintainers

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws when `safeParse` fails, so any `.success` check on its return value is redundant/dead. This redundancy is visible in `packages/app-store/office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` where the code still does `tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data`. However, there are no Zoom changes/usages of `parseRefreshTokenResponse` shown anywhere in the provided diff, so the finding’s claim about “Zoom callers” is not verifiable from this diff and is therefore not accurate as stated.

adjudication_records.issue_text: refreshOAuthTokens parameter is typed as () => any, leaking untyped returns into all callers and losing the original typed return values

adjudication.rationale: Yes. In the new file `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts`, the helper is declared as `const refreshOAuthTokens = async (refreshFunction: () => any, appSlug: string, userId: number | null) => { ... }`. Because the callback is typed `() => any` and the function has no generic/explicit return type, TypeScript will infer an `any`-based return (`Promise<any>`). That means callers (e.g. `const hubspotRefreshToken: HubspotToken = await refreshOAuthTokens(...)`) lose compile-time checking of what is actually returned and `any` can flow through. This is a verifiable type-safety defect introduced by the diff, regardless of runtime behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: refreshOAuthTokens sync-endpoint branch returns raw fetch Response without checking response.ok, conflating transport success with valid token response

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts`, when `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT && userId` is true, the function does `const response = await fetch(...); return response;` with no `response.ok`/status check and no parsing/validation of the body. That means a 4xx/5xx (or other transport-level failure that still yields a Response) is returned to callers as if it were a valid token refresh result. This is a verifiable defect in the diff (and some callers, e.g. GoogleCalendarService, treat the return value as if it contains token data).

adjudication_records.issue_text: Office365Video passes app slug 'msteams' to refreshOAuthTokens while living under office365video/ directory, potentially causing 404 in credential sync webhook

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "msteams", credential.userId)` in `packages/app-store/office365video/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts`. However, nothing in the diff establishes that the correct app slug for the Office365 video integration is *not* `msteams` (directory name ≠ app slug). There’s no shown mapping (e.g., `appStoreMetadata` entries) or other code indicating the expected slug, so the claim that this will cause a 404 in a credential sync endpoint is speculative and not verifiable from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: App slug strings are hardcoded at each refreshOAuthTokens call site instead of using a single source of truth like the app's config.slug

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show multiple call sites passing string literals as the `appSlug` argument to `refreshOAuthTokens` (e.g., "google-calendar", "hubspot", "lark-calendar", "office365-calendar", "msteams"). However, this is not a verifiable bug/correctness/security defect introduced by the diff: nothing in the shown code indicates these literals are wrong or inconsistent with the actual app slugs, nor is there an available “single source of truth” in scope at these call sites to prove the hardcoding causes incorrect behavior. This is primarily a maintainability/DRY suggestion rather than a concrete problem evidenced by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is string | undefined instead of boolean, risking mistakes like === true comparisons always being false

adjudication.rationale: The diff only shows `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` being imported from `@calcom/lib/constants` and used in boolean contexts (`if (!APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED)` / `if (APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && ...)`). The diff does not show the definition or type of `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED`, nor does it introduce any `=== true` comparisons. Therefore the claim that it is `string | undefined` (and that `=== true` comparisons would always fail) is not verifiable from this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: parseRefreshTokenResponse return type mismatch causes Google Calendar credential corruption in CalendarService.ts

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`, the function returns the full Zod `safeParse` result object (`{ success, data, ... }`), not the parsed token/credential data itself. In `packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts`, the code assigns `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema);` and then persists it via `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`. Previously it stored `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)` (the actual credential object). With the new code, the stored credential `key` becomes the wrapper safeParse result rather than the credential payload, which will corrupt the persisted credential shape and likely break later code expecting `credential.key.access_token`, etc.
